clue.text: What greedy types have sadly doesn't start to go away — so, in truth, it's disgusting!

indicators.note: something done sadly is done badly, so the letters are jumbled into a new order
the first letter of the word doesn't is told to leave, so its opening letter is dropped

parts.note: the cry of disgust Ugh! sums up 'it's disgusting'

explanation.surface: Someone moaning about a greedy attitude that refuses to go away, and saying in truth it's revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to go away' drops the D of DOESN'T to leave OESNT; 'sadly' shuffles that with SOINTRUTH to make SNOUTSINTHETRO, and UGH finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom pictures pigs feeding greedily, used of people grabbing money or perks, so the greedy have their noses in a feeding vessel.

clue.text: Cash needed to keep up a British institution, initially

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the hidden run is read from the bottom upwards
the words Cash needed keep the letters within them, a signal that they hide a run of letters

explanation.surface: A plea that a beloved British institution needs money to keep it going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to keep' hides SHN across 'caSH Needed'; 'up' turns it round. 'initially' tells you the definition wants the institution's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The National Health Service is Britain's state health system, known by its three initials.

clue.text: Bright? Not when head's gone

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which here has gone

parts.note: a place lit by the sun is bright

explanation.surface: A wry answer to whether someone is clever: not once they have lost their head.
explanation.walkthrough: Behead SUNLIT, a synonym of 'Bright', and what is left is the opposite of bright, which the whole clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Without any lighting a room is dark, the opposite of bright, as the clue's question and answer suggest.

clue.text: Battle of Britain? Let me think (one with many stories to tell)

definitions.text: one with many stories to tell

parts.note: the 1940 Battle of Britain was fought in the air, a scrap in the sky
er is the hesitation sound of someone thinking

explanation.surface: Someone asked about the Battle of Britain pauses to recall a veteran full of war stories.
explanation.walkthrough: The Battle of Britain was the 1940 air war over southern England, hence a fight (scrap) in the sky. 'stories' are the floors of a building, not tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A very tall building has many floors, and storeys are spelt stories in American English, giving the pun on telling tales.

clue.text: A Sierra! Wrong about Clarkson's last car

indicators.note: about means everything before it, the A, the Sierra letter and the wrong, is turned round

parts.note: Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a wrong is a sin

indicators.note: the last letter of the name Clarkson is taken

explanation.surface: Jeremy Clarkson, the British TV motoring presenter, reviewing a Ford Sierra and getting it wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sierra was a Ford family car, a red herring here: it only supplies S. Clarkson presented the car show Top Gear.
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese manufacturer makes motor vehicles, so its brand name stands for a car.

clue.text: Endlessly rebel against exploitation — calm down!

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to rebel against is to defy
exploitation is use of something

explanation.surface: A protester raging against exploitation is told to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebel' is a verb here, and 'against' is only a link meaning 'next to'.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the heat out of a tense situation, as with a bomb, is a verb meaning to make calmer.

clue.text: Leaving university, coming out with this?

definitions.text: Leaving university, coming out with this?

indicators.note: the letter for university leaves the word

parts.note: a debut is a first appearance, a coming out

explanation.surface: A question about what graduates take away when they leave college.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove U from DEBUT and the whole clue describes what students carry away from their studies.
explanation.definitionFit: Graduates typically finish their studies owing large student loans, money still to be repaid.

clue.text: Shamefully common places giving poor support, essentially

definitions.text: Shamefully common places giving poor support, essentially

parts.words: Shamefully common places giving poor support, essentially
parts.note: the places are charities handing out groceries, support for the poor with essentials; 'poor support' reads as weak help

explanation.surface: A complaint that shamefully many venues give inadequate help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor support' looks like criticism, but means support for the poor, and 'essentially' points to the basic groceries handed out.
explanation.definitionFit: Charity centres distributing free groceries to people in need have become widespread, which many think a national shame.

clue.text: Effort unrewarded — left in bar at party

indicators.note: in says the letter for left goes into the word for bar

parts.note: bar and save both mean except, as in 'all bar one'
Labour is one of the main UK political parties

explanation.surface: Someone stuck working in a bar at a party for no pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like a pub but means 'except', which is SAVE. Labour is a British political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Work exacted without pay, as from enslaved people, is effort that goes unrewarded.

clue.text: See 24
Blast out rocks — not the full amount

indicators.note: rocks means shakes violently, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Instructions to blast out rocks, though the job is only partly done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocks' looks like the object of the blasting, but it is the verb that shuffles BLAST OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A partial total, added up before the final figure, is not the whole sum.

clue.text: Dives with power to crap — occasionally gull slightly worried tour leader

indicators.note: something worried is worked at or disturbed, so these letters are rearranged
occasionally picks only every other letter of the word gull
the leader of the word tour is its first letter

explanation.surface: A seagull swooping to foul a tour party, leaving its guide a little anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives is the rich man in Jesus's parable of Dives and Lazarus. 'occasionally' takes UL from GULL; 'leader' gives T of TOUR; 'slightly worried' shuffles them with TOCRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Dives, the biblical rich man, stands for wealth; a wealthy person who also holds power is one who rules through riches.

clue.text: Provided for Ellie splashing out — why one's very easily led

indicators.note: splashing out suggests letters flung about and rearranged

parts.note: provided means if, as in 'provided it rains'
the letter Y is pronounced like the word why

explanation.surface: Ellie being treated lavishly, and someone asking why she's such a pushover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'easily led' suggests a gullible person, but it is a life that is led very easily.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a carefree, comfortable existence, a way of living with no hardship.

clue.text: Be back at bottom (experienced recession)

indicators.note: back means the word Be is read in reverse

parts.note: a bed is the bottom of a river or sea

explanation.surface: An economist noting a return to rock bottom during a recession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recession' sounds economic, but here it is water receding.
explanation.definitionFit: When the tide went out it receded, so the past tense of a verb for flowing away fits experiencing recession.

clue.text: To save, I grant, was difficult with these

definitions.text: To save, I grant, was difficult with these

indicators.note: difficult here signals the letters are put into an awkward new order

explanation.surface: A concession that putting money aside was hard on such meagre pay.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifteen letters of TO SAVE I GRANT WAS rearrange, and the whole sentence describes the pay that makes saving hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Pay too small to live on leaves nothing to put by, so saving was difficult with it.

clue.text: Businessman with nothing? Judgment needs reversing

parts.note: FA, short for sweet Fanny Adams, is British slang for nothing

indicators.note: the word for judgment needs to be read backwards

parts.note: tact is good judgment in dealing with people

explanation.surface: A businessman with nothing whose bad decision has to be overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet FA' is British slang for nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A wealthy, overpaid executive is a well-known idiom for a rich, self-satisfied boss.

clue.text: See 1
Lines in road, ones round new zone

parts.note: ST, for street, is a road

indicators.note: round means the two As go around the other letters

parts.note: A means one, so ones gives two As

explanation.surface: Road markings: lines painted around a new zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines in road' suggests road markings, but 'Lines' alone is the definition, verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of lines forming a unit of a poem is a verse.

clue.text: Began to write in reference book

indicators.note: in places the word for writing inside the dictionary's initials

parts.note: the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
to pen is to write

explanation.surface: Someone starting to write inside a reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Began to write' looks like one phrase; 'Began' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Started and its synonym in the past tense, as when a shop or a meeting got going.

clue.text: Others in work turned over very quickly

indicators.note: in puts the others inside the reversed work
turned over means the word for work is flipped round

parts.note: OP, for opus, is a work
the rest are the others

explanation.surface: Colleagues at work flipping something over in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' as OP (opus) is a standard abbreviation; 'turned over' reverses only that piece, not the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: In music it is the Italian tempo marking for a very fast pace, also used for anything done instantly.

clue.text: Get back from Uncle Ed's in about eight minutes (tops)

indicators.note: in puts the name inside the word for about

parts.note: re means about, as in a letter heading
Ed is the name, with 's standing for is

indicators.note: tops picks the top, first, letter of each word

explanation.surface: Collecting something from a relative's place within eight minutes at most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is old British slang for a pawnbroker, not a relative; 'tops' looks like 'at most'.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying back a pawned item from the pawnbroker is the classic sense of reclaiming a pledge.

clue.text: Financier (or crook) holding over ten million in Delhi

indicators.note: over means the hidden run is turned round
the words holding a run of letters hide it within them

explanation.surface: A crooked financier hoarding a vast sum of rupees.
explanation.walkthrough: ERORC lies across 'financiER OR Crook'; 'over' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: In South Asian counting, this unit equals one hundred lakh, a number used for rupee sums.

clue.text: Selfish speech involving quarrel over old school subject

parts.note: selfish talk is all about me

indicators.note: involving means the reversed quarrel goes inside

parts.note: speech is talk

indicators.note: over means the word for quarrel is turned round

parts.note: a row is a quarrel

explanation.surface: A self-centred speech that ends in an argument about something taught at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns the quarrel round, and 'involving' puts it between the last two letters of the speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaping and joining metal was taught in many schools as a craft class, now largely dropped.

clue.text: See 14
Has meekly compromised over current British businessman

indicators.note: over means the anagram sits over, around, the letter for current
compromised means damaged, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A tycoon who has meekly given ground in a dispute over current affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of HAS MEEKLY wraps round I.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the English founder of the Sports Direct retail empire and a former owner of Newcastle United football club.

clue.text: Sham! Sick country, one has to conclude

parts.note: ill means sick
US is a country
I've is short for I have, one has

explanation.surface: An exclamation dismissing a sick nation as a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one has' read as 'I have' gives I'VE; 'to conclude' puts it at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deceptive, based on illusion and unreal, is a fake or pretence.

clue.text: Artist reduced access

indicators.note: reduced means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: ingress is a way in, access

explanation.surface: A painter complaining that their entry has been restricted.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was a French Neoclassical painter.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a celebrated 19th-century French painter, hence an example of an artist.

clue.text: She's always short

definitions.note: the definition is She, with 's for is

indicators.note: short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: A remark about a woman who is never tall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' looks like her height, but it trims EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Eve is the first woman of Genesis and a woman's name, so it can stand for she.

clue.text: Fruit harvest originally stops school in Provence

indicators.note: stops means plugs, so the letter goes inside the school

parts.note: a lycée is a French secondary school

indicators.note: originally takes the first letter of harvest

explanation.surface: The harvest shutting a French school, as farm work takes over.
explanation.walkthrough: H plugs LYCEE, the French word for a secondary school.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small Chinese fruit with a rough red shell and white flesh.

clue.text: Politician with reduced brainpower tries to spin

indicators.note: reduced means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the mind is brainpower

indicators.note: to spin means to turn about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dim politician who tries to put a spin on things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spin' suggests political spin-doctoring, but it shuffles TRIES to ISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A government member in charge of a department is an elected official, so one kind of politician.
